overview: Kamerun was a German colonial territory imposed on diverse African societies from 1884. The map shows its enlarged outline near the First World War; its 1914 to 1920 display interval does not mean German rule lasted until 1920.

periods.title: Colonial conquest and resistance
periods.summary: German colonial control expanded inland from the coast.

periods.title: An enlarged colonial claim
periods.summary: A Franco-German agreement added the territories called Neukamerun.

periods.title: War reaches communities

periods.title: Partition and mandates
periods.summary: British and French occupation preceded the League of Nations mandates.

items.text: The coastal agreement of 12 July 1884 preserved cultivated land and town sites for their existing owners and successors, and promised respect for local customs. Those clauses matter: people accepting an agreement had expectations about homes and authority that German colonial expansion would violate.

Rubber and cocoa connected Kamerun to European factories, but the work could be brutal. Concession companies used forced labor, while military expeditions destroyed villages and seized land for plantations. A chocolate bar or rubber comb had a much longer human story than its shop label revealed.

A British cable connected the colony to the international telegraph network in 1893. A separate German connection through Togo followed in 1913. A coastal message could now cross an ocean without waiting for a ship to deliver the words.

sections.title: A schoolboy becomes a defender of homes

items.text: Rudolf Duala Manga Bell learned German at a government school and, beginning in 1891, spent five years studying in Germany. He succeeded his father as a Duala leader in 1908. His education later helped him address the colonial authorities and reach readers and politicians overseas.

From 1911 the authorities forced land seizures and relocation in Duala. Their plan separated African and European residential areas with a strip one kilometer wide. For families, colonial racism meant losing familiar homes and neighborhoods, not simply seeing a different flag above an office.

Manga Bell used petitions and allies in the German press and parliament. In March 1914, a petition helped persuade the Reichstag to withhold funds for the expropriations while examining complaints. The authorities then prosecuted him in an unfair trial and executed him on 8 August 1914.

sections.title: Writing, family letters and learning in Bamum

items.text: At Foumban, King Ibrahim Njoya and his scribes developed the Bamum script beginning around 1896. Its early signs included animals, body parts, foods and household objects. They repeatedly revised the system; in 1910 it was reduced to about seventy signs. This was an African intellectual achievement within the colonial era.

Surviving works from the script’s 1906 to 1908 phase include letters between Njoya and his mother and an agricultural calendar. Writing served family conversations and the farming year as well as royal affairs. Even a king could receive a letter from his mother.

Learners recited the Bamum signs in a fixed sequence, with pairs that often rhymed or shared an opening consonant. That gave memory a pattern to hold onto. In 2006, researcher Charles Riley also found the healer Zakari Nkepu teaching with a brush-written chart at his workplace.

Here are the first four signs of the modern Bamum recitation sequence: ꚠ ꚡ ꚢ ꚣ, read “a, ka, u, ku.” They are syllables, like the beginning of an alphabet recital, rather than a sentence. These are standardized digital forms of the signs.

A small language sample is “Ŋga nsapŋam,” the Latin-transcribed title of a Bamum proverb collection attributed to Njoya and published in 1987. Riley identifies the volume as “Collection of Bamum Proverbs.” This is a modern printed witness to that literary tradition; the displayed letters transcribe Bamum rather than reproduce its distinctive script.

sections.title: War and the end of German rule

items.text: The First World War campaign depended on African soldiers on both sides. Cameroonian recruits knew forest and mountain routes, built defenses and supplied local fighting skills. The fighting was not simply a contest between a few European officers: local knowledge helped determine where armies could move and survive.

Recruitment and advancing troops drove civilians from their villages. Early in 1915, thousands of refugees gathered around Allied posts at Edea and Kribi; other people hid in the bush or ended up in plantation camps. The collapse of German control brought partition, not immediate independence for these communities.

ending.text: German control ended in the 1914 to 1916 campaign, with resistance at Mora lasting into February 1916. British and French administrations divided the territory; Germany renounced its colonial rights in 1919, and League mandates followed in 1922. The imported 1920 endpoint marks neither independence nor the disappearance of Cameroon’s peoples.
